difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the new antibiotic reduces mortality in the trial, agree side effects are non-trivial, and agree resistance is a concern. The disagreement is implicit: Tanaka's reasoning commits her to the view that the trial's mortality benefit should govern approval now, while Ruiz's commits him to the view that it should not, because resistance risks are a current decision-input, not a future one. Trap (B) is agreement in disguise; (D) swaps 'current decision' for 'future prescribing'.
stimulus: Dr. Tanaka: The phase III trial showed a thirty-percent drop in mortality from drug-resistant pneumonia, and the side effect profile, while not trivial, is manageable with monitoring. The agency should approve the drug on that record. Future resistance is a real worry, but it is a worry about what comes next, and can be handled through prescribing guidelines. Dr. Ruiz: A thirty-percent mortality reduction is significant, and I would not dispute the safety data. But broad approval will drive the very resistance we are both concerned about, and once that resistance is entrenched, no prescribing guideline will undo it. The trial result tells us the drug works today; it does not tell us we should authorize it today.
questionStem: Dr. Tanaka and Dr. Ruiz are committed to disagreeing over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the risk that broad approval will accelerate resistance is a sufficient reason to withhold approval now

choices.label: B
choices.text: the drug reduced mortality from drug-resistant pneumonia in the phase III trial

choices.label: C
choices.text: prescribing guidelines can completely eliminate the risk of antibiotic resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: physicians should restrict their prescribing of the drug once it has been approved

choices.label: E
choices.text: the drug's side effects rule out approval on safety grounds alone

explanations.correct: Tanaka treats resistance as a downstream worry handleable by guidelines, so it is not a reason to withhold approval now; Ruiz treats resistance as the decisive reason to withhold approval now. Piecing together their full statements, they are committed to opposite yes/no answers on exactly this proposition.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Tanaka asserts it and Ruiz calls it significant.
explanations.C: Neither speaker claims complete elimination; Tanaka only says guidelines can handle it, and Ruiz denies guidelines would fix entrenched resistance, not that they aim to eliminate it.
explanations.D: The dialogue is about whether to approve, not about post-approval prescribing behavior; neither speaker takes a position on what individual physicians should do after approval.
explanations.E: Both speakers agree the safety data is acceptable; Tanaka calls side effects manageable and Ruiz says he would not dispute the safety data.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the defendant lied under oath, agree the lie was material, and agree a conviction would be legally sustainable. The disagreement is whether the prosecutor was ethically required to bring the charge, which has to be reconstructed from Lund's 'duty to pursue' reasoning and Abebe's 'discretion to decline where the social cost exceeds the marginal deterrent gain'. Trap (C) is an apparent disagreement that dissolves; (E) is a shift of subject.
stimulus: Lund: The defendant lied under oath about a material fact. A prosecutor who has uncontested evidence of perjury has a duty to pursue that charge; the integrity of sworn testimony depends on people knowing such lies will be prosecuted. Whether a jury convicts is a separate question. Abebe: The evidence here was uncontested, and yes, a conviction would almost certainly have been sustained on appeal. But prosecutorial resources are finite, and when the marginal deterrent value of one more perjury case is small compared to the cases it displaces, the office is entitled to decline. That is not a failure of integrity; it is a judgment about where public harm is greatest.
questionStem: Lund and Abebe's statements commit them to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: a prosecutor faced with uncontested evidence of material perjury is ethically required to bring the charge

choices.label: B
choices.text: the defendant's false statement concerned a material fact

choices.label: C
choices.text: prosecutorial offices operate under genuine resource constraints

choices.label: D
choices.text: a perjury conviction in this case would have been sustained on appeal

choices.label: E
choices.text: declining to prosecute the case would weaken public trust in sworn testimony

explanations.correct: Lund asserts a duty to pursue perjury where the evidence is uncontested; Abebe asserts the office is entitled to decline when deterrent value is low. The two positions cannot both be held.
explanations.B: Both speakers grant materiality — Lund asserts it and Abebe does not contest it.
explanations.C: Only Abebe invokes resource constraints; Lund takes no position either way on whether such constraints exist, only on their relevance.
explanations.D: Agreement in disguise — Lund implies a conviction was available and Abebe concedes it would likely be sustained.
explanations.E: Lund implies integrity is served by prosecution, but does not claim declining would weaken trust; Abebe's view is that declining is not a failure of integrity. Neither speaker commits to the specific trust-erosion claim.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the Phillips curve has weakened empirically and both agree that low unemployment has coincided with low inflation in the last decade. The disagreement is implicit: Haugen treats weakened correlation as evidence the underlying mechanism is gone, while Desai treats it as evidence the mechanism is masked by favorable supply conditions that may not persist. Trap (A) is agreement in disguise; (D) is out of scope.
stimulus: Haugen: For most of the past decade, unemployment has been historically low without any meaningful pickup in inflation. The Phillips curve, which predicted exactly such a pickup, has lost its predictive grip, and central banks should stop designing policy around a relationship that the data no longer bears out. Desai: I grant that the simple textbook curve has been a poor forecaster recently. But that stretch coincided with uniquely favorable supply conditions — globalization, flexible labor markets, stable commodity prices. Those conditions are fading. Writing off the underlying relationship now is exactly the wrong lesson to draw from a decade of good luck.
questionStem: Haugen and Desai's statements provide the most support for the claim that they would disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Phillips curve has been a poor empirical forecaster over the past decade

choices.label: B
choices.text: the relationship between unemployment and inflation the Phillips curve describes still operates as an underlying mechanism

choices.label: C
choices.text: supply-side conditions over the past decade have been unusually favorable

choices.label: D
choices.text: central banks' current policy frameworks should place more weight on commodity prices

choices.label: E
choices.text: low unemployment has coincided with low inflation in recent years

explanations.correct: Haugen treats the weakened correlation as evidence the underlying relationship is gone; Desai explicitly resists 'writing off the underlying relationship' and attributes the weakness to temporary conditions. That is a direct disagreement about whether the mechanism still operates.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Haugen calls the curve's predictive grip lost and Desai grants the textbook curve has been a poor forecaster recently.
explanations.C: Only Desai takes a position on supply-side conditions; Haugen does not address them.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on commodity prices as a policy input; Desai only cites stable commodity prices as one favorable condition.
explanations.E: Both speakers accept this — Haugen states it outright, Desai does not dispute it.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree carbon pricing reduces emissions, both agree regressive effects on low-income households are real, and both agree dividends can be paid. The disagreement is about whether dividends fully neutralize the distributive objection — Olander treats dividends as sufficient; Ibarra treats them as insufficient because the harm is not only in aggregate income but in exposure timing. Trap (A) is agreement; (E) is out of scope.
stimulus: Olander: A carbon price reduces emissions efficiently, and the revenue can be rebated as equal per-person dividends. Once you do that, the typical low-income household comes out ahead in net terms, because their direct carbon footprint is smaller than average. The distributive concern about carbon pricing is, for practical purposes, solved. Ibarra: Aggregate net-positive numbers hide a timing problem. The price rise hits heating, gas, and groceries immediately every month, while the dividend arrives quarterly or annually. A family living paycheck to paycheck is not made whole by a refund that shows up after an eviction notice.
questionStem: Olander and Ibarra are committed to disagreeing over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: a carbon price reduces emissions

choices.label: B
choices.text: equal per-person dividends funded by carbon pricing revenue adequately address the policy's distributional impact on low-income households

choices.label: C
choices.text: the direct carbon footprint of low-income households is smaller than the population average

choices.label: D
choices.text: carbon pricing dividends should be paid monthly rather than less frequently

choices.label: E
choices.text: the government should expand heating subsidies independently of any carbon pricing scheme

explanations.correct: Olander concludes the distributive concern is for practical purposes solved by equal dividends; Ibarra's paycheck-to-paycheck counter is precisely that dividends do not adequately address the impact. Piecing together each speaker's full statement is required.
explanations.A: Both would agree; Olander asserts it and Ibarra does not contest it.
explanations.C: Only Olander invokes this claim; Ibarra does not address the comparative footprint.
explanations.D: Ibarra highlights the timing mismatch but does not explicitly advocate monthly payments; Olander does not address payment frequency at all. No clear yes/no disagreement.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker takes a position on heating subsidies as a separate program.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree restoration is feasible in principle, both agree the watershed has been severely degraded, and both agree native species have declined. The implicit disagreement is whether restoration is worth doing given the baseline question: Quince treats the pre-dam ecosystem as the operative target; Reyes treats it as an arbitrary benchmark not entitled to special authority. Trap (C) is an apparent disagreement that evaporates; (D) is one-sided.
stimulus: Quince: The dam has transformed the watershed, and native salmon runs are down by over ninety percent. Dam removal is engineering-feasible now, and a decade of restoration would let the river return to something close to its pre-dam condition. Given what we have lost, that outcome is clearly worth pursuing. Reyes: I agree removal is feasible, and I do not contest the decline figures. But 'pre-dam condition' is just the state the river happened to be in when someone started measuring. Restoring it favors the species that were dominant then over the species that are dominant now, and I see no reason the earlier configuration has a stronger claim on us.
questionStem: Quince and Reyes disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: dam removal on this river is engineering-feasible at present

choices.label: B
choices.text: restoring the pre-dam ecosystem would succeed on ecological grounds

choices.label: C
choices.text: native salmon populations have declined by over ninety percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: the current species composition of the watershed should be preserved as it now stands

choices.label: E
choices.text: the pre-dam ecosystem is the appropriate target for restoration of this watershed

explanations.correct: Quince treats pre-dam condition as the outcome clearly worth pursuing; Reyes explicitly denies that the earlier configuration has a stronger claim on us than the current one. Each speaker's full argument has to be integrated to see this.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers grant feasibility.
explanations.B: Neither speaker questions ecological success on its own terms; the dispute is whether that target is the right one.
explanations.C: Both accept the decline — Quince asserts it and Reyes does not contest it.
explanations.D: Only Reyes implicitly defends the current configuration; Quince takes no position on preservation as an independent goal.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree recommendation algorithms shape what users see, both agree platforms make editorial-like choices, and both agree user autonomy matters. The implicit disagreement is whether users' revealed consent to opaque ranking defeats an autonomy-based objection — which requires combining Kuroda's 'consent via continued use' with Ferreira's 'consent presupposes the very transparency the system withholds'. Trap (A) is shared; (D) is shift of subject.
stimulus: Kuroda: Every platform that ranks content is making editorial choices; that is unavoidable. Users know this in broad outline, and they continue to use the platforms. Continued use under roughly accurate public descriptions of how ranking works is the kind of consent that settles the autonomy objection to algorithmic curation. Ferreira: Platforms do make editorial choices, and autonomy is exactly what is at stake. But the 'broad outline' users have is a press release, not a mechanism. Meaningful consent to being ranked requires knowing what is being optimized and how, and that is precisely what users are not told. What you are calling consent is compliance.
questionStem: Kuroda and Ferreira's statements most strongly support the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: recommendation algorithms make choices analogous to editorial decisions

choices.label: B
choices.text: users' continued use of ranked platforms under current disclosure practices constitutes consent sufficient to defeat the autonomy objection

choices.label: C
choices.text: users currently know the precise optimization targets of recommendation algorithms

choices.label: D
choices.text: platforms should be legally required to publish their ranking source code

choices.label: E
choices.text: autonomy is a consideration that any evaluation of algorithmic ranking must take into account

explanations.correct: Kuroda says continued use under broad public descriptions settles the autonomy objection; Ferreira says that what Kuroda is calling consent is merely compliance and does not defeat the objection. Each speaker's position has to be assembled from multiple sentences.
explanations.A: Both agree platforms make editorial-like choices.
explanations.C: Both would deny that users know the precise optimization — Kuroda says users have only a broad outline and Ferreira agrees that is all users have.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on publishing source code; the dispute is about consent, not disclosure remedies.
explanations.E: Agreement in disguise — Kuroda frames his argument around the autonomy objection and Ferreira explicitly says autonomy is at stake.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the newly discovered letters are authentic, both agree the conventional account of the treaty's origins has explanatory gaps, and both agree the letters fill some of those gaps. The implicit disagreement is whether the letters warrant overturning the conventional account: Balan treats filling gaps as sufficient; Ostrow treats it as insufficient absent corroboration from independent sources. Trap (A) is agreement; (E) is a shift.
stimulus: Balan: The newly discovered Hartwell letters are authentic, and they fill the awkward gaps in the standard account of the treaty's negotiation — especially the chancellor's silence in the spring of 1827. Historians have been working around those gaps for a century; the letters supply what was missing, and the standard account should be revised accordingly. Ostrow: The letters are genuine, and yes, they plug exactly the gaps you name. But a single correspondent writing from one side of the negotiation is not enough to rewrite the record. Until the Hartwell material is corroborated by sources outside his circle, the most we should say is that a rival account is now plausible, not that the standard one is wrong.

choices.label: D
choices.text: corroboration from sources outside Hartwell's circle would strengthen any revised account

choices.label: E
choices.text: the treaty's terms as signed differ from those the chancellor originally favored

explanations.correct: Balan concludes the standard account should be revised accordingly; Ostrow concludes that the most we should say is that a rival account is plausible, not that the standard one is wrong — a direct denial of the revision conclusion.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers affirm authenticity.
explanations.C: Both accept this — Balan names the gap and Ostrow says the letters 'plug exactly the gaps you name.'
explanations.D: Only Ostrow invokes corroboration as a standard; Balan does not take a position on whether further corroboration would strengthen a revision.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the debate is about whether to revise the account, not about the chancellor's preferences over terms.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree grammaticality judgments shift across speakers, both agree some shifts reflect change in progress, and both agree that 'standard' usage is partly a social artifact. The implicit disagreement is whether prescriptive judgments ever track a genuine property of the language rather than social positioning. Arriaga says yes (where a construction violates a deep pattern common to most dialects); Pell says no. Trap (C) is shared; (E) is one-sided.
stimulus: Arriaga: Many prescriptive rules, I grant, are just prestige dialect dressed up as grammar. But not all of them. When a construction violates a pattern that shows up in nearly every dialect of the language — say, a word-order constraint that every speaker I have tested respects below the level of awareness — calling that construction ungrammatical is tracking something real about the language, not scoring social points. Pell: Speakers' judgments shift, and what most dialects now share was once shared by fewer. 'Respected by most speakers below awareness' is a description of current distribution, which is itself a social fact. I see no version of 'genuinely ungrammatical' that is not, in the end, a statement about whose usage currently counts.
questionStem: Arriaga and Pell disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: some prescriptive rules reflect prestige dialect dressed up as grammatical rules

choices.label: B
choices.text: any classification of a construction as ungrammatical can track a property of the language rather than a social fact about whose usage counts

choices.label: C
choices.text: grammaticality judgments can shift across generations of speakers

choices.label: D
choices.text: word-order constraints are operative in every dialect of the language

choices.label: E
choices.text: speakers' current usage has the same authority as their grandparents' usage

explanations.correct: Arriaga gives a case where ungrammaticality tracks a genuine property of the language; Pell asserts he sees no version of 'genuinely ungrammatical' that is not a social fact. Resolving this requires reading across each speaker's reasoning.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Arriaga concedes it and Pell plainly endorses it.
explanations.C: Both accept this — Pell asserts judgments shift and Arriaga does not dispute it.
explanations.D: Arriaga hedges to 'nearly every dialect' and Pell does not take a position on universality; no clean yes/no disagreement.
explanations.E: Only Pell hints at this; Arriaga does not address generational authority.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the work is aesthetically accomplished, both agree the artist held views most would find odious, and both agree the views influenced the work's content. The implicit disagreement is whether aesthetic merit can be evaluated independently of the moral defects expressed in the content. Merton says yes (craft and content separate at the level of evaluation); Salazar says no. Trap (A) is shared; (D) is shift.
stimulus: Merton: The novel is, on any ordinary craft measure, a major achievement — structurally daring, prose of extraordinary control. Everyone grants the author's published views were repellent, and those views do shape what the characters argue. But the quality of the book as a made thing is one judgment, and the moral content it carries is another, and we evaluate them separately. Salazar: Structural daring, prose control, yes. And the views inflect the characters' arguments, as you say. But the book's architecture is built around a sympathetic portrait of those same views. The craft is not hovering above the content; it is how the content is made persuasive. You cannot rate the craft high and the content low and call yourself done.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the aesthetic quality of the novel can be evaluated separately from the moral content the novel expresses

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: novels whose authors hold repellent views should be removed from school curricula

choices.label: E
choices.text: the views of the author shape what the characters of the novel argue

explanations.correct: Merton treats the quality judgment as one thing and the moral content as another, evaluated separately; Salazar says you cannot rate craft high and content low and call yourself done — i.e., the two cannot be evaluated separately. That is the implicit yes/no axis.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Merton calls the views repellent and Salazar does not contest it.
explanations.C: Both agree the prose has extraordinary control.
explanations.D: Out of scope — neither speaker takes a position on curricular inclusion.
explanations.E: Both accept this — Merton says the views shape what characters argue and Salazar agrees the views inflect the characters' arguments.

difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the firm's conduct was legal, both agree it caused significant harm to a third party, and both agree the harm was foreseeable. The implicit disagreement is whether foreseeable but lawful harm to a third party triggers moral obligation to compensate — which requires combining Essien's 'legality is the limit of enforceable duty' with Yavuz's 'foreseeability plus causation grounds a moral duty even where law is silent'. Trap (C) is agreement; (D) is a shift.
stimulus: Essien: The firm operated within every rule on the books, and the harm to the downstream community, while real and foreseeable, resulted from conduct no regulator had chosen to prohibit. Where the law draws the line is where enforceable duty ends; beyond that, you may disapprove, but you may not demand payment. Yavuz: I will stipulate the conduct was legal and that the harm was foreseeable — those are precisely my premises. If a firm knowingly acts in a way that predictably injures an identifiable third party, the absence of a statute does not dissolve the obligation to make that party whole. A duty is not only what a legislature has written down.
questionStem: Essien and Yavuz are committed to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: a firm has a moral obligation to compensate a third party for foreseeable harm caused by conduct that is not prohibited by law

choices.label: C
choices.text: the harm caused to the downstream community was foreseeable at the time the firm acted

choices.label: D
choices.text: legislatures should enact new statutes prohibiting the firm's type of conduct

choices.label: E
choices.text: regulators have been lax in not prohibiting the firm's conduct

explanations.correct: Essien holds that beyond the law's line you may not demand payment — a denial of obligation to compensate; Yavuz holds the absence of a statute does not dissolve the obligation to make the injured party whole — an affirmation. The pieces have to be assembled from each speaker's full argument.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers stipulate the conduct was lawful.
explanations.C: Both accept foreseeability — Essien calls the harm real and foreseeable and Yavuz stipulates the same.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on future statutes; the debate is about obligation given the current legal landscape.
explanations.E: Only Essien implicitly defends the regulators by saying no regulator chose to prohibit; Yavuz does not take a position on regulator conduct.
